title: Decadal Amplification of Wildfire‐Induced Perturbations in Summer Surface Energy Partitioning Across the Boreal Forest Biome
content:
Abstract

Wildfires fundamentally reorganize the surface energy balance of boreal forests, yet the temporal evolution of these perturbations under rapid Arctic amplification remains insufficiently understood. Integrating multi-source remote observations, climate reanalysis, and a potential outcomes framework, we quantified decadal trends in fire-induced summer surface energy partitioning across multiple successional stages for the entire boreal biome from 2005 to 2024. Our results revealed a significant decadal amplification of fire-induced perturbations, signaling a transition toward a novel biogeophysical state increasingly dominated by sensible and ground heating. Specifically, anomalies in latent heat flux and combined sensible and ground heat fluxes exhibited significant trends of −0.24 and 0.26 W m−2 yr−1 during the 1-year recovery period, and −0.18 and 0.18 W m−2 yr−1 by the 7-year successional mark. Temporal attribution identified escalating summer dry-hot climate anomalies, specifically rising vapor pressure deficit and temperature, as the predominant drivers constraining evapotranspiration (ET) and suppressing recovery. This climate-driven mechanism was exacerbated by escalating high-severity fires, which facilitated near-complete combustion of the canopy, maximizing net radiation absorption while severely reducing ET capacity. Crucially, we identified a critical regulatory role of functional stagnation in vegetation recovery by year 7, highlighting a fundamental shift from disturbance-dominated to climate- and recovery-limited controls on energy partitioning. These responses underscore a self-reinforcing feedback loop that exacerbates near-surface warming and atmospheric aridity, further suppressing regrowth and prolonging moisture deficits. Our findings necessitate integrating these accelerated biogeophysical dynamics and shifting recovery baselines into Earth system models to accurately project high-latitude climate-fire interactions.
